life_summary: Amasa Mason Lyman was born in 1813 and became a prominent leader during the Church's formative years. He was introduced to the faith by missionaries in spring 1832 and baptized on April 27, 1832. Lyman participated fully in the Church's westward expansion, helping to establish the San Bernardino settlement in California, where he served as the settlement's first mayor. He purchased land as part of the Rancho San Bernardino acquisition and contributed to Mormon colonization efforts in the West. His family became influential within Church leadership circles, with descendants who achieved prominence in subsequent generations.
church_summary: Lyman joined the First Quorum of the Seventy in 1835 and served as regent of the University of Nauvoo in 1841. Joseph Smith called him to the apostolate in 1842 and appointed him as an additional counselor in the First Presidency in 1843. Following Smith's death, Lyman supported Brigham Young's leadership and participated in the 1847 westward migration. However, his Church status declined after he preached doctrinal positions at odds with established teaching. The Church stripped him of apostleship in 1867 and excommunicated him in 1870 for associating with dissident groups, though he was posthumously reinstated in 1909.
